C001.name: Differential programming
C001.definition: A programming paradigm where parts of the program are parameterized and gradient-based optimization tunes the parameters to optimize the program or find a local optimal.

C002.name: Representation learning
C002.definition: This is a major topic where the class will look at reconstruction based and similarity based methods, along with the theory of representation learning.

C003.name: Reconstruction based
C003.definition: This is one of the methods the class will look at when studying the theory of representation learning.

C004.name: Similarity based
C004.definition: This is one of the methods the class will look at when studying the theory of representation learning.

C005.name: Transfer learning
C005.definition: This is the process of pre-generating representations that can be learned upon without needing to learn everything from scratch.

C006.name: complex phenomena
C006.definition: These are things that students interact with every day, such as natural language, images, visual data, videos, DNA, ecosystems, or climate change.

C007.name: Perceptron
C007.definition: The first neural network, which was intended to recognize or categorize images.

C008.name: Backpropagation
C008.definition: The concept that enables multilayer perceptrons by allowing a gradient to be propagated through multiple layers of perceptrons.

C009.name: Multilayer perceptrons
C009.definition: Multiple perceptrons stacked on top of each other to be reasonably trained.

C010.name: XOR problem
C010.definition: A categorization problem that cannot be solved by a linear classifier.

C011.name: AI winter
C011.definition: A period where enthusiasm for machine learning took a dip because the ability to train models efficiently was lacking.

C012.name: ImageNet
C012.definition: The first very large-scale data set of its kind.

C013.name: Non-linearity
C013.definition: Non-linearity refers to the simple non-linearity placed between two different layers of the model.

C014.name: Gradient descent
C014.definition: The idea that we are trying to optimize some cost function by finding a minimum set of parameters where the loss is minimized for all of the training data points.

C015.name: Theta
C015.definition: The set of all the parameters of the model, which includes the set of all the weight terms and all the bias terms.

C016.name: Linear layer
C016.definition: A component of the output representation in that linear layer, which is a sum over input components of some weight times each of those input components, plus a bias term.

C017.name: Nonlinear function
C017.definition: A function that maps your outputs, which is necessary because a neural net must be more than just linear combinations of inputs.

C018.name: Stacking layers
C018.definition: The process of taking a single version of the linear projection and non-linearity and stacking another one on top of it.

C019.name: Parameters of our model
C019.definition: The parameters of the model are all the different layers of weights and all the different layers of biases.

C020.name: Non-linear classification
C020.definition: Non-linear classification is the ability to perform classification using a deep net, even if that deep net is only a two-layer perceptron.

C021.name: Double-layer model
C021.definition: A double-layer model is a structure built with two layers, which is used to demonstrate non-linear combinations.

C022.name: Representational power
C022.definition: This refers to the ability of a network structure to represent any function, provided it has sufficient capacity and non-linearity.

C023.name: Capacity
C023.definition: Capacity is the number of parameters in the model, which includes both the width and the depth of the network.

C024.name: Overparameterized
C024.definition: This describes a model that has so many parameters that, classically, it would be expected to overfit the training data.

C025.name: Double Descent
C025.definition: This is a modern interpolating regime where models, even when massively overparameterized, can achieve better performance after passing an interpolation threshold.

C026.name: Abstracted representations
C026.definition: These are representations that become more complex as the network progresses through increasing layers.

C027.name: Overfitting
C027.definition: Overfitting occurs when a model learns something too spiky or too peaky to fit the training data perfectly, causing it to generalize worse.

C028.name: Cross-entropy loss
C028.definition: Cross-entropy loss is a function that indicates the distance between what the model believes the output distribution should be and what the input distribution actually is.

C029.name: One hot encoding
C029.definition: One hot encoding is a vector that is 0 everywhere except for the place where it is correct, where it is 1.

C030.name: Tensor
C030.definition: A tensor is a multi-dimensional matrix, serving as the mathematical representation of the model's input data.

C031.name: Batch
C031.definition: Batch processing allows for the parallel calculation of individual losses for data points, which are then summed efficiently.

C032.name: Deep networks
C032.definition: Deep networks are a more compact way of representing knowledge in data.

C033.name: Low-level representations
C033.definition: These are representations in earlier layers that categorize things like directional orientations of light and dark gradients in the pixels.

C034.name: Complex representations
C034.definition: These are representations in later layers that get combined into more and more complex concepts.

C035.name: Weight reuse
C035.definition: This is the idea of reusing components of previously trained models to achieve efficiencies in training.

C036.name: Loss
C036.definition: The loss is calculated based on the difference between what the model predicts and the ground truth.

C037.name: Parameters
C037.definition: Parameters are associated with each layer of the neural network and are the values that are getting learned.

C038.name: Getting learned
C038.definition: Getting learned essentially means wiggling the values around in numerical space until they are reasonably close to optimal based on available data.

C039.name: Optimal set of theta
C039.definition: The optimal set of theta is the set of parameters that minimizes the loss function over all of the available data set.

C040.name: Cost function
C040.definition: The cost function is the sum of the loss over all the data points in the training data set.

C041.name: First order optimization
C041.definition: This is optimization where we know that we can evaluate the gradient of theta.

C042.name: Local minimum
C042.definition: A minimum that may not be guaranteed to be the global minimum if the loss landscape is non-convex.

C043.name: Learning rate
C043.definition: The learning rate, eta, specifies how far we are going to step in the direction of that gradient.

C044.name: Parameter update
C044.definition: This is the change to parameters resulting from moving them in the direction of the maximal slope of the gradient with some learning rate step value.

C045.name: Gradient
C045.definition: These are the values computed with respect to the weights during the parameter updates.

C046.name: Overall loss function
C046.definition: This is the function that ideally needs to be minimized, which is calculated as a sum of the individual losses over every single example in the training data.

C047.name: Stochastic gradient descent
C047.definition: This method assumes that taking the gradient over a subset of the data is a reasonable approximation to taking the gradient over the entire data set.

C048.name: Standard gradient descent
C048.definition: This is the method used when the batch size is equal to N, which is the full set of data.

C049.name: Implicit regularizer
C049.definition: The noise generated by stochastic gradient descent acts as an implicit regularizer.

C050.name: Local minima
C050.definition: These are points where the optimization might end up, depending on where you start, but which are not the global minimum.

C051.name: Momentum
C051.definition: In gradient descent, momentum biases gradient steps to continue in the direction of the previous update, based on its past direction of movement.

C052.name: Hyperparameter
C052.definition: The strength of momentum, represented by alpha, is a hyperparameter.

C053.name: Adam optimizer
C053.definition: Adam is a popular example of a type of momentum used in gradient descent.

C054.name: Autograd
C054.definition: It is a nice mechanism that helps us calculate gradients for any function.

C055.name: Exploding gradients
C055.definition: This is a challenge where the gradient is really large as you get close to the minimum, causing the optimization to bounce far away.

C056.name: Differentiable
C056.definition: A property where every single one of these nodes can have a derivative calculated.

C057.name: vanishing gradient
C057.definition: This occurs when the progress of optimization is very slow, and noise in the batches might end up dominating over the signal.

C058.name: multiple local minima
C058.definition: A situation where the loss landscape is not guaranteed to have only a single local minimum.

C059.name: Evolution strategy
C059.definition: It is a gradient-like method that finds locally loss-minimizing directions in parameter space by sampling small perturbations around existing parameter values and moving towards the perturbations that achieve lower loss.

C060.name: Gradient clipping
C060.definition: It is a mechanism that helps with peakiness or pointiness in the loss function by scaling back the gradient if it gets too high above some large value.

C061.name: Loss function
C061.definition: Loss functions are the functions used to measure the error, and they can sometimes have negative values depending on how they are set up.

C062.name: Gaussian Error Linear Unit
C062.definition: GeLU is a function that takes the parameters times phi of the parameters, where phi is the cumulative distribution function for the Gaussian distribution, and it is everywhere continuous, differentiable, and smooth.

C063.name: Activation function
C063.definition: Activation functions are the functions used within the neural network structure.

C064.name: Computation graph
C064.definition: A graph of different functional transformations.

C065.name: Directed
C065.definition: Means the information only goes one direction on any given edge.

C066.name: Acyclic
C066.definition: Means you don't have loops or cycles.

C067.name: Forward pass
C067.definition: The process of taking in input values and parameters and mapping through a functional transformation to get outputs.

C068.name: Derivative of output with respect to input
C068.definition: If the output y is a scalar, the derivative with respect to the input x is a row vector where each element is the partial derivative of y with respect to a specific element of x.

C069.name: Jacobian formulation of the partial derivative
C069.definition: When y is a vector of size n by 1, the partial derivative with respect to x results in a matrix of size m by n, where m is the size of y and n is the size of x.

C070.name: Partial derivative of y with respect to matrix x
C070.definition: If y is a scalar and x is a matrix, the partial derivative of y with respect to x will be a matrix of size m by n, where each component corresponds to a relevant component of x.

C071.name: Chain rule
C071.definition: For a function h of x being f of g of x, the derivative is the product of the derivative of f with respect to g of x and the derivative of g with respect to x.

C072.name: Multiplication of two partial derivatives
C072.definition: In the context of the chain rule, the derivative can be written out as the multiplication of two partial derivatives.

C073.name: Partial derivative
C073.definition: This is the value needed to calculate the update in parameters, such as the partial derivative of j with respect to theta 1.

C074.name: Backwards pass
C074.definition: This involves sending the error signal, the gradients, and the loss backwards through the network from the outputs to the inputs and parameters.

C075.name: Validation set
C075.definition: This set is used to monitor training progress by looking for some sort of plateauing of change.

C076.name: Input gradient
C076.definition: The input gradient is essentially the output gradient multiplied by the update to those parameters with respect to the input.

C077.name: Weight update
C077.definition: The update to the weights is calculated by multiplying the input to the function by the output gradient.

C078.name: Cost
C078.definition: Cost is the overall calculation of the loss over all of the data or a subset of the data.

C079.name: Backward for a linear layer
C079.definition: The backward operation for a linear layer is the same operation as the forward pass but with the weights transposed.

C080.name: Gating matrix
C080.definition: A gating matrix is a mechanism that turns the ReLU into, parameterized by the activations from the forward pass, to ensure gradients are not passed for components that were masked out by the ReLU.

C081.name: First order approximation of the derivative
C081.definition: This approximation involves fitting a plane to a complex curved loss landscape, which is the essence of moving in the direction of the plane.

C082.name: Single big linear model
C082.definition: The entire process, encompassing both the forward and backward passes for a linear model, can be treated as one single, large, flipped-out linear model.

C083.name: Intermediate representation
C083.definition: The intermediate representation is the value of the embedding at each layer that must be saved in memory during the forward pass so that backpropagation can be efficiently computed.

C084.name: Embedding
C084.definition: An embedding is a neural network that maps a high-dimensional or complex input, such as an image, to a low-dimensional representation or vector.

C085.name: Directed-acyclic graph
C085.definition: This is the structure that allows for arbitrary connections in machine-learning models, which can be handled by merging and branching operations.

C086.name: Merging
C086.definition: When propagating a gradient back through a merge, you must track the gradient with respect to the correct input variables.

C087.name: Branching
C087.definition: When propagating a gradient back through a branch, the gradient is calculated by summing the gradients from both paths and sending that sum back through the input.

C088.name: Parameter sharing
C088.definition: This is when the parameters are reused across different components of a network, such as reusing pre-trained parameters.

C089.name: Software 2.0
C089.definition: This concept defines a space of possible software systems, allowing optimization within that space to build the required system to solve a problem.

C090.name: Feature engineering
C090.definition: Feature engineering is essentially building a bunch of explicit constraints into how the data might be processed before it goes through a simple neural network.

C091.name: CLIP
C091.definition: CLIP is a model that tries to make descriptions and images that correspond to them close together in a joint embedding space.

C092.name: Merging operation
C092.definition: A merging operation is a simple operation required to translate backpropagation from MLPs to any Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).

C093.name: Branching operation
C093.definition: A branching operation is a differentiable operation that represents any structure in a DAG, such as splitting an embedding vector.

C094.name: Universal function approximator
C094.definition: A statement that neural networks can approximate any function that is of interest.

C095.name: Optimization
C095.definition: The question of whether one can find the function that exists within the model family.

C096.name: Generalization
C096.definition: The question of whether the model performs well on data that has not been seen before.

C097.name: ReLU
C097.definition: ReLU is the function used to approximate the hyperrectangle functions.

C098.name: Weierstrass' function
C098.definition: It is a function that is everywhere continuous but nowhere differentiable.

C099.name: Pathological function
C099.definition: It is a classic example of a function with unusual properties.

C100.name: Family of curves G
C100.definition: These are the curves that we want to be able to approximate ideally.

C101.name: L-infinity error
C101.definition: This is the maximum discrepancy between the two functions anywhere on the input space.

C102.name: L1 measure
C102.definition: This measure is the integral over the input space of the absolute value of the difference between the two functions.

C103.name: Lipschitz continuous function
C103.definition: It is a particular notion of continuity.

C104.name: L-Lipschitz
C104.definition: A function is L-Lipschitz if the amount the function changes when the inputs change is bounded by the Lipschitz constant times the size of the input change.

C105.name: RMS norm
C105.definition: The RMS norm of a vector is defined as the square root of 1 over d times the sum of the coordinates xi squared.

C106.name: L-Lipschitz functions
C106.definition: These are functions that map from the hypercube to the real numbers and are characterized by having bounded derivatives.

C107.name: Hypercube
C107.definition: It is an abstract way of writing down a d-dimensional space where all axes are constrained to be between 0 and 1.

C108.name: Integral notion of error
C108.definition: This error is calculated by summing up all the absolute values of the difference between the neural net and the function g.

C109.name: Number of units
C109.definition: This refers to the total number of neurons in the ReLU MLP.

C110.name: Universal approximation theorem for a single value layer
C110.definition: This theorem states that in a single layer, given a certain amount of value units, one can approximate a function to arbitrary precision.

C111.name: Hyperrectangle
C111.definition: This is the multidimensional generalization of the rectangle construction that the network aims to approximate.

C112.name: Three-layer ReLU network
C112.definition: This is a specific network architecture to which a particular result applies.

C113.name: Indicator
C113.definition: It is a function which is 1 if the input is in the interval, and 0 otherwise.

C114.name: Approximation error
C114.definition: The approximation error is bounded by the Lipschitz constant divided by 2 times the number of strips.

C115.name: error cap
C115.definition: This is the part of the hyperrectangle where the hyperrectangle differs from the surface G.

C116.name: area
C116.definition: This is the surface area of each hyperrectangle, which is calculated to be 1 over N when summing all hyperrectangles.

C117.name: Approximation
C117.definition: This refers to the process of using a network structure to represent or mimic a target function, such as a rectangle.

C118.name: Two-layer ReLU network
C118.definition: This is a network structure capable of approximating functions, such as a rectangle or a square function.

C119.name: Constant c
C119.definition: This constant is used as a weight to increase the slope of the curves within the network construction.

C120.name: Combining ReLUs
C120.definition: This is the technique of using multiple ReLU functions together to construct a more complex shape.

C121.name: Three-layer network
C121.definition: This is the final network structure achieved by adding a linear combination layer on top of the hyperrectangle construction.

C122.name: Riemann sum
C122.definition: This is the context where a two-layer network is used to approximate each individual rectangle.

C123.name: Hyperrectangle function
C123.definition: These are the functions, referred to as bumps, that the network is attempting to approximate.

C124.name: Generalization performance
C124.definition: This refers to the network's performance on unseen data, which is claimed to be poor when fitting data using tiny strips.

C125.name: Number of neurons
C125.definition: This refers to the count of neurons used in the construction, which determines the 4D term.

C126.name: Width versus depth
C126.definition: This is a question concerning whether it is better to scale the width or the depth when designing a neural network model.

C127.name: Compositionality
C127.definition: The ability of a network to create a richer space of functions by combining multiple nonlinearities through function composition.

C128.name: Parallelism
C128.definition: The advantage of a wide network structure that allows the system to make better use of parallel hardware.

C129.name: Feature representations
C129.definition: The outputs of the network layers that are easier to interpret and are considered 'nicer'.

C130.name: Arbitrary nonlinearity
C130.definition: The complex functions that a network can approximate using pointwise nonlinearities and function compositions.

C131.name: Depth separation results
C131.definition: A theoretical result showing that a deep network can represent a particular function efficiently, whereas a shallower network would require exponentially more neurons.

C132.name: Piecewise linear
C132.definition: A function that is composed of multiple linear pieces.

C133.name: Linear regions
C133.definition: A property of a piecewise linear function that refers to the number of linear pieces it contains.

C134.name: kink
C134.definition: A kink is the number of discontinuities in the derivative, or the number of places where the derivative suddenly changes.

C135.name: KINKS-L
C135.definition: KINKS-L denotes the maximum number of kinks over the n coordinates of the output of layer L.

C136.name: Deep ReLU network
C136.definition: A deep ReLU network is a network structure where the function at layer L is defined recursively as ReLU of the weight matrix times the function from the previous layer plus the bias.

C137.name: Layer L
C137.definition: The function at layer L is defined as ReLU of the weight matrix times the function from the previous layer plus the bias.

C138.name: Width
C138.definition: The width (n) is the dimension of the n-dimensional vector and the size of the n by n weight matrix.

C139.name: Depth
C139.definition: The depth (L) refers to the number of layers in the network.

C140.name: Explicit construction
C140.definition: An explicit construction is a method, such as using a small ReLU network, that demonstrates that a theoretical upper bound can actually be attained.

C141.name: Triangle function
C141.definition: The triangle function is a specific function defined as a small ReLU network that, when composed with itself, recursively doubles its structure.

C142.name: Depth separation
C142.definition: Depth separation is the phenomenon where a simple function requires an extremely wide shallow network but can be achieved with a much smaller depth.

C143.name: Test loss
C143.definition: The y-axis in the figure that is always going down as you scale the compute, data set size, or number of parameters.

C144.name: Allocation of compute budget
C144.definition: The distribution of compute resources between network width and depth, which the paper claims does not matter within several orders of magnitude.

C145.name: Confounders
C145.definition: An aspect of the training pipeline that is not fully understood but is having a bearing on the experimental results.

C146.name: Chinchilla scaling rules
C146.definition: A set of rules that question some of the results found in earlier scaling papers.

C147.name: Wide shallow neural net
C147.definition: A wide shallow neural net, such as a three-layer MLP that is wide enough, can fit any function within a broad class of functions.

C148.name: Inherent two-dimensional structure
C148.definition: This refers to the structure present in image data.

C149.name: Inherent sequential structure
C149.definition: This refers to the structure present in waveform data.
